blocks.x: Okay. You want to hear what it was on?
Yeah, just go on.

What's your name? Well, sure, Paul. I'll be happy to. My name is Don Albert, professionally, and my family name is Dominique. I imagine you know of my uncle in Chicago. He still uses his name Dominique. His name is Natty Dominique, one of the first trumpet players to leave from New Orleans along with King Oliver and the other guys. And after this, where you are now, we're in San Antonio, Texas. This is my residence, and it's 715 St. James. Been living here for the last five years in this home. We bought this after we returned from New Orleans in 1950.
This is June the 6th, 1961, and I'm Paul Crawford. You were talking about this fellow, one of the first guys you took, you know, when you left New Orleans? No. A banjo player or something?

Yes, I remember that real well. And right here's a picture of him, Paul. Richard McCarthy. I was 16 years old, and Richard I think was 17 or 18. We were in the same bracket there. And then we also had another fellow just a little older, maybe about six or seven months. His name was Johnson. What did he play? He was the alto player. Uh-huh. That was the three that I took out of New Orleans that year going to Dallas.
Did you have a job when you left New Orleans or what were you doing?

Yes, we had a job off of us. We didn't know whether we were good enough for it or not because we only knew how to play three songs. What, do you remember what the three were? I Love You, The Sheik of Arabi were two of them. I can't remember the third one. But anyhow, after we got to Dallas, then there was a band traveling with me on the same train. It was the year that the New Orleans Pelicans were playing Wichita Falls in the Classic. And the fellas in this band, the T&T band, with some great musicians, later on I had the opportunity of playing with one of the greatest tenor saxophone players that ever played. And incidentally I helped him along in his music career later on when I got in Troy Floyd's band. I'm referring to the great Herschel Evans. So we were on this train coming into Dallas and the guys made me play my horn all night. On the train because they loved to hear the tone that I got out of the trumpet then. And I remembered well the other song was the Indian Love Call. And I played the Indian Love Call until I got sick. And over here is when I first got my band Paul. I was twenty-one years old, twenty years old here. You notice the difference? A big head of hair. Yeah. Fowlly good looking fella. Yeah. And this is... With stripy pants. That's right. Gambling striped pants. That's correct.
I remember seeing a picture of Duke Ellington wearing pants like that.

Well this was the style in those days. And this whole outfit was made by one of the best tailors in Dallas through one of the bookers, the man that found me, Bernard Goldberg. This other picture you see here is later on when I had stopped playing I was only featuring myself on two or three numbers. I had to take care of the business of the band. This was taken in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. And naturally this one here that you're looking at I was eight years old. This is in my backyard. You notice the wash tubs? Uh huh. This is at 1719 North Robeson Street, New Orleans, Louisiana. I think in this picture I'm eight or nine, not over ten years.
That's a nice old style horn.
That's a nice old voice. Well the guys had a nickname for me, 1776. 1776. In response to this horn.
The old horn.
That's right.
Yeah.

Are there any particular questions that you would like to ask me concerning any of the music career or pictures I'd be happy to show them to you? This one here Paul, I'm also somewhat of an actor on the stage. I played in about five or six major productions, that is locally. Was offered a part in Deep of the Roots on Broadway but didn't accept it. This picture here is Dark Tower. A very, very fine play directed here by Mrs. Myra Hemings. I had the leading role in that also.
And when did you start acting?

Oh ever since I was a little boy I used to act around with the wonderful piano player, Wilhelmina Bartz, her sister, I can't remember her name, right? Gertrude I think it was. We were kids together and we acted on the stage. And in my school days, Valina C. Jones, I acted on a couple of plays there. Of course naturally after I got my band together I deviated from the stage until I settled here in San Antonio and I complied everything that I knew just as the hobby.
So you must have been, that acting ability must have been good, you know, in good stead for MCing and being the band director. It must have been made it good, huh?

Yes it did. It fit in just like a glove on the hand I imagine. Of course now I've had a varied life. I've thanked the Lord for many things that he blessed me with. Being a musician there's all the things that I could do. As you know I'm now working at Randolph Field.
What do you do out there, Don?

I'm a packer and creator for overseas shipments of engines and parts for the planes. Uh huh. Then there's a lot of other things that I have done in the line of work which makes everything come easy. It isn't hard when my music played out on me for me to get into some type of work to make myself a fairly good living. Happily married to the same woman for 31 or 32 years, but I love to tell the people it's over 65 because it seems it's been that long.
You told me the other night you got married two weeks ago or something.

Did you believe that? No. She changed it didn't she? This is my daughter, my last child. She's eight years old now. You see various stages of her life. She's danced on the stage since she's been a little top one year old. I had her dancing for the soldiers when I'd go out there and entertain them. I've done a lot of that work for them.
Is this about as old as she is now?
No, she was six years old here. She sure is a pretty child.
A little feminine. Very talented.

Yes, very talented and well raised and she has all good traits about her. Very smart in school, makes all A's and B's. This is my mother that was taken out at Lake Punch and Train one year that I went to visit them. Oh yeah. You recognize that? That's the seawall. That's the seawall. Yeah. My mother passed not so long thereafter. She was seventy, seventy-three years old. My dad is still living.
Yeah, Bill said he's still living but he won't talk to him. Well, he's a peculiar fellow.

He probably didn't know. I told Bill he had the wrong approach. He should have told him first that he knew Don Albert and then that would have been all. He'd have talked the rest of the night with him. This, Bill, is when I was in New York playing with my band. I was about twenty-three then. I was one of the first band leaders to use this set of tails, colored tails. This was incidentally blue. And this is my nightclub here with one of the big nights. There's over six hundred people in here this time. You notice that the crowd is mixed. It's an integrated crowd. I'm also a pioneer in this type of business. Same as I was in the jazz field. That's good. Yeah.
What is that? Is that somebody? No, that's the man you met the other night in the apartment. Oh yeah, yeah.
I guess he sort of looks a little bit like Beans.
He does. Well Beansy was here, Beansy met him.
Incidentally both of them in the same. Now here's the band that I left New Orleans with, Paul. Yeah.
I know you want to see this. Now we'll try to recall some of these names. I'll help you.

This is Ferdinand Davis. I'm sure you don't know him. I know his name. Yes. He was confined to the hospital in Baton Rouge and he passed about two or three years ago. This is Arthur Durbany. He's still living. Great alto player. Wonderful. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. This is- Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Oh yeah? All fine trumpet. Yeah. But he played sax with you. Sax with my band. And double on the trumpet. This is the greatest drummer that I've ever heard in my life, Albert Martin. And that's saying a lot because I've heard all of the drummers in those days. Joe Jones was tops also. I think that Phat was far greater than Joe Jones ever was. Naturally you know this fellow here, he's in all of the old- That's Johnson? That's Jimmy Johnson.
Yeah.

Jimmy passed years ago in New Orleans. The last job he played with me was in Mobile, Alabama. This fellow you wouldn't know him. He was the first addition to the Ten Pals. This is Howe Harding. He's now in Dallas. Uh huh. He's still alive then? He's still living. He's uh-
Yeah, he'd be fairly- he wouldn't even be in his late 40s you think? No, no.

He would be older than I am. Oh yeah? Howe Harding would be around 55. Uh huh. Although I guess you know this fellow in the middle, right? Yeah, that's you. That's you. Kind of nice-looking fellow there. Yeah, I know he is. He's only 20 years older. Almost the tallest one in the bunch.
Tallest one. Well you're stooping then.
Yeah, I'm taller than Hall. Yeah. This is Herbert Hall. He's now in New York. He's with Jimmy Condon.
Uh huh.
And his brother, of course you know him don't you? Hall was with-
Edmund. I met Edmund once. I don't know him real well but I remember he had a Jaguar car.

Now this fellow, you recognize him? That's Cartrell. That's correct. This fellow you wouldn't know. He is from a little town in Louisiana, Lake Charles. This is Frank Jack here, the trombonist. Uh huh. You notice there's only one trombone in this band before the band increased. It was only three brass. Two trumpets and a trombone. This is Al Freeman from Columbus, Ohio. The pianist and arranger. Marvelous piano player. Wonderful arranger. Sight reader. And this is Sidney Hansel, another New Orleans boy. He was the vocalist. You notice in those days we didn't have microphones as we have now, speakers. So he had to use this old megaphone. You notice the megaphone, sing after megaphone. We used all these instruments that you see here. Hall double on the baritone. These are the two trumpets.
Yeah.
The first trumpet here, my trumpet is a CG con that was presented to me when they first made them. The first long con trumpet that was made. Uh huh. Now that's the original band.
That was after the ten uh...

No this is the Ten Pals. Uh huh. And that was the first name of the band. America's greatest swing band came in after I increased the band. Now here is a picture here. I told you I did a varied amount of entertaining. These are convalescent soldiers at Fort Sam Houston that have been overseas and came back for some reason or another day and incapacitated some kind of way. And I'm entertaining them there with the show and the band from the Keyhole Club.
Uh huh.
And I put more people in here than any other entertainer's ever been in here. You know, to stay all on the top.
Uh huh.
You said that Dick Allen had asked you to get a few questions for me?
Yeah. You said that uh... A few questions and he wanted me to tell you a few things. That's mighty fine. Or maybe you could tell me about Bill Phillips.
Bill Phillips, my drummer? Yeah. Oh man, sure, I'd be happy to. But before I do that, this is my son here that was serving in the Korean War.
Uh huh.

This is Kenneth. Is he here? He's here, but he's over at his house with his wife. I believe Bill met him. Yes. He came in just as Bill was completing the interview. And he is 31 years old now. Did he play anything? No, he never did want music. Now we'll get back to Bill Phillips. That is the first band that I actually played with and he was the cause that my professor stopped teaching me. Bill Phillips came to get me to play with his band and my professor didn't think that I should play in a band but he had never mentioned it to me. So when I came to take my lessons one night he told me, he says, well I don't think you need any more lessons now. You're a finished musician. I heard you playing in a band. Well from that I went on out and of course I had a very, very good knowledge of music because I had studied under Milford Piron for almost two years without an instrument just reading music out of a book and beating the time with my hand and reading the music as it was and singing it. For how long you did that? Almost two years. No kidding. That's right. That's why Paul, I'm not ashamed to say it, I don't know whether you noticed or not, but I'm not afraid to put anybody's music in front of me and read it at sight. I don't say that I'll play it perfect but I will play it.
Was Milford Piron akin to AJ?
That's AJ's older brother. I see. Piron is cousin, Armand Piron is cousin to me through marriage.
Well Dick said to tell you that Bill Phillips is a bass drummer now with the Young Tuxedo Brass Band.
Oh he is? Fine.
And he has a vegetable truck and he's doing very well.

Good. I visit Bill every time I go to New Orleans and Ida always fixes what I used to like to eat over there and every time I go there I say, Don, I've got your dish cooked for you. What's that? Dumbo and rice. Yeah. That's right. And I go over there and Bill just stacks up my automobile with all the fruit. Oh yeah? And I can't pay him for it. I try to pay, he says no you don't pay. Probably hit you with his bass drum beater. And he also played my wedding. See when I left New Orleans I was a kid but I was engaged to my wife and when they announced the wedding, well Bill got all of the musicians to, I didn't even know they were going to do that, and they gathered in the house at 1677 North Mero Street that night at eight o'clock. And they all played and they weren't satisfied until I sat in the band to play something with them. So you know on my first wedding night I didn't want to play too much. No. But I did play a little. I think that was kind. That's right. But Bill Phillips always been a very, very great friend of mine. I've always admired Bill Phillips because he's been a gentleman ever since I've known him.
Now did you tell me what your motto was? You did, didn't you, the greatest swing band?

Oh well that was in later years Paul. You see originally my band was named Don Albert and his 10 Pals. Some said 10 Happy Pals. But I don't ever remember that I called it the Happy Pals but since they said it was that, it didn't interfere too much with the name. It's already 10 Pals. Yeah. And we were happy to be together and I said make the name all right. But in later years as I increased the band I'm the first one that used the word swing. And a lot of times it was misinterpreted. People would say what do you mean a string band? I said it's not string band, swing band. But what do you mean? And I would try to give the definition of the type of music that we played. That everybody was swinging when we played. And we just said America's greatest swing band. And then it stuck until the band went down. Who took the solos in the Troy Floyd band? I took most of the solos but Willie Long played the solo on the Shadowland Blues. But all the other solos in the band, the trumpet solos, I played most of them. And Sykai Collins played the alto solos and then there was Scott Bagby played the clarinet solos. Until Herschel came into the band. Of course Troy has had a lot of other members in his band after I left. He changed them like the weather.
You said you knew Buddy Petit?

Oh yes, I was a very good friend to Buddy. I think I recall telling Bill Russell an incident about Buddy and I. I used to play on this boat they call the Susquehanna. I don't know if you can recall that. You probably weren't nowhere around New Orleans. I read the name. You read the name? Yeah. Well the Susquehanna would leave Spanish Fort and go across the lake and it would dock over in, what's the name of the little town over there? Vanderville? Northern. Covington? Covington. And the doctor, it would dock there on and I would jump off the boat and the first thing I would do I'd run out in the country to where Buddy was. And actually I'd find him in his house where he was and he'd be sitting down and he'd be running over his horn or eating something. He'd always get a kick out of me being there because I was a little kid. And actually I admired anybody who played a trumpet because I wanted to learn. And I'd sit down and talk to Buddy two and three hours at a time until the time for me to get back to the boat. And actually I wasn't drinking because I didn't know what drinks was. I was only about 13 or 14 years old. And when I'd finish talking with Buddy, and actually I'd get back on the boat and when it would dock I'd have to rush home to beat the nine o'clock bell. Because the old man would be waiting.
Do you remember anything about his style? Like you know, was he a high note man?

No, not a high note man. In those days trumpet players didn't play high notes. They had more of a running style. You mentioned the trumpet player the other day, Punch. Punch Miller. Do you remember Punch Miller? Sure. Well Punch Miller to me is as near to playing the style that Buddy played than anybody else that I heard. A style similar to what he's playing. Now Punch, don't misunderstand me, now Punch isn't copying Buddy PT. He's playing his style. But he gives you an idea what Buddy actually played. Oh he was fine, the tone was so beautiful. Was he fast? Very fast. Very fast. He had a good tone. Very beautiful tone. Well the same way I mentioned Chris Kelly, a lot of guys said that Chris Kelly could only play two or three songs I have to disagree. Now he did play Loveless Love like nobody else played it. He created something of his own style and later on whether they say it or not, Cootie Williams adopted what he was doing with the Flushy. Of course Cootie did more with it than what he was doing. But it stems right from what he was playing. And I mentioned that to Bill Russell, I really enjoyed, I used to enjoy listening to those two fellas playing. The tones were so beautiful.
Oh, there's something else that I told you I saw, I was talking to Emmanuel Sales the other day.
Oh yes, that's your player?
Yeah. Fine. He said to tell you that he thinks that Cottrell and a couple other guys, a trio recorded a tune that you and Cottrell wrote. And one of the names was True.

Do you remember that? Do you have another name? That was the theme song. The actual title of the song is You Don't Love Me. Now Paul Gayton is the one that changed the name from You Don't Love Me to True.
Oh he did.

That was later then. That is correct. Much later. That's when it was first recorded. Paul Gayton is the one that put it on. Then later on I got Camille Howard to play it but she played it in the wrong vein. She played it in the jump tempo and You Don't Love Me isn't a jump song. It was the theme song of the band. Cottrell, myself and Lloyd Glenn. The pianist that was in my band. He came after Freeman didn't he? Long after Freeman. Yes he came quite a while after Freeman. I think that, I'm not for sure I think there was, no he might have been the one after Freeman. Then there was Lionel Reason, that's another pianist that's playing now. And I think that was the three pianists that I had. Freeman, Lloyd Glenn, oh no, Jay Golson. He was the arranger. He's in Detroit now, a tremendous arranger.
You had a regular arranger for your band?

There was five fellas in the band that arranged at one time. Harold Holmes later on when Jimmy Johnson was getting a little slow, we added Harold Holmes to the bass section. We also had a tuba, so we had a tuba, two bass fiddles in the band at the same time. Harold Holmes wrote the arrangements, another terrific trumpet player that I picked up in the eastern states, Billy Douglas. He, unfortunately he was, oh he liked to hit the bottle too much we say. But he would have been one of the mighty, mighty greats for what he could play. He did arranging. Then later on I had Jay Golson, then Lloyd Glenn did arranging. Cotrell wrote a few arrangements, Herbert Hall wrote some. Then I had Philander Tiller out of Little Rock, Arkansas that wrote sensational arrangements and he couldn't play them himself after he wrote them. Did Cotrell tell you that? No, no.
But I'm just agreeing that I do some of that myself.

That's peculiar, isn't it? Arthur Dabney, Cotrell, Hall, and Philander Tiller. Philander would write sensational parts for the Reeds and we would have to rehearse Philander for maybe a week for him to learn his part. Of course that's how the band had so many original arrangements. We never transferred arrangements with any other band. We didn't ask any other band to give us arrangements or did we exchange arrangements with any bands.
You sure must have a lot of enthusiasm in the band to have that many arrangers.

Well Paul, you talk about enthusiasm. We would ride 250 and 300 miles in the old raggedy bus on the highway and get to town, wash up and get a little breakfast and go to rehearsal. Some guy would be writing arrangements all the way to the next town and then have to go to work that night and travel the next night. Is that enthusiasm? Sure has. My real name is Lawrence Douglas. I'm L.D. Harris. My real name is Lawrence Douglas. I'm L.D. Harris.

I'm born and raised in Brenham, Texas. That's about 165 miles from here. It's on H and TC between Austin and Houston, Texas. And I started out playing music between the ages of 13 and 14, started studying music. They organized a boys band there. I had a fellow who had been in the service by the name of Gus Allen. He was a boy band. He was a boy band. He was a boy band. Something to keep us off the street I guess, keep us off the devil. So they did. And I was a boy band. I was a boy band. I was a boy band. I was a boy band. So they did. And they put me on the alto horn. And I went from that alto horn to the valve trombone. And then I got ambitious and wanted to play the slide trombone. And I went off and played the slide trombone. It got me pretty good. And every summer, after I got about 15 years old, every summer from then on until I was about 18, my father would let me go down to Houston and play with Sid Iles. Sid Iles had this whole Southwest tied up. And he was from Texas, all Texas, part of Louisiana, New Mexico tied up. He just mentioned his name and that was it. He'd get a crowd. And he let me go down and play with him. Well I learned the business of managing a band and how to lead a bunch of fellas and learn something about. In those days they had, the bands were kind of on a, you had brass bands that played. John Jones. John Jones. John Jones.
Want to go there? One time? Yeah.

I want to hear that myself. Well now let's see, I was telling you about going down to Houston there. And I learned to lead a bunch of fellas, what the responsibilities was, and did pretty good after that. I started. And I went off with a left here and left Sid Iles, and went off with a carnival, carnival show. The boys said they were going down to Mexico and I'd never been to Mexico and I wanted to get away and go down to Mexico. So I just forgot about school and went on down there. The old man Sid Iles, he had promised the old man to take care of me like a father, which he did. I lived right in the house with him there. And he wouldn't give me my clothes. And the only way I could get my clothes, I had to write a letter and put it inside another envelope and tell the boy, a friend of mine, when you get this to mail it to the old man, tell him I'm at home. So he'd send my clothes home. I sent them home to my mother. I got my mother to send them to me after he sent them home to her. So that's where I got my clothes. I got my mother to send them to me after he sent them home to her. So that's where I got my clothes. I got my mother to send them to me. So I stayed down there now. I got my mother to send them to me after he sent them home to me. That's where I got my clothes down in Mexico. I stayed down there now. I made good down around the border. I'm down in the border right now, Texas Valley down there. So I came on back, back to Houston again, got barred with Houston again. And we organized a band there called the Alexander's Ragtime Jazz Band. Old Dave Alexander, we named it after him. He was well known. He worked on the Ice Truck and things around there. Well known a lot of people, a lot of other people, a lot of other people. Kind of felt like they keep you laughing all the time.
About what year was that? That was long about 1921.

Yeah, about 21, maybe about 1920. Anyway, we all got this band and we got lots of work. We just got to clean up right now. A fellow by the name of Freeman Mitchell was booking bands. He had a little capital because he worked at the roundhouse for the S.P. Railroad Company. He had a little money to invest and he was lucky with it. And he paid us well. We opened up the Arts Brothers Temple. We opened up the Pilgrim Hall and played there. We got to be, I'll tell you how popular we were. We got so popular that Duke Ellington was playing there at the Pilgrim Temple. We were playing down there for Don Robie. Don Robie, he had this place, what's the name of that place, Don? Harlem Grill. Harlem Grill. He was operating this Harlem Grill and we head out playing down there. We closed Duke up. When the red light would go on, then you start to record it. Now the man in the back that's recording it, there was a little light thread would come off of that disc and it would pile up and then you'd have to wrap it up and take it off and throw it on the floor. And that was one continuous operation until you cut the disc. And then the lights would go on and nobody said a word, nothing dropped on the floor, you couldn't breathe too hard. That's right. Today it's a lot different.
That's the way it was now we made our first records. We were so crazy about the records we even saved that little, that little shave in it, Lucas. And I kept that for a long time.
Look at that I made records, you don't believe it, look at this other thing.
Yeah.
